chapter_theme: Saccandan's body is burned while Kattiyankaran weeps false tears and the king's women mourn and vow to follow him; the mechanical peacock carries Vijayai down into the burning ground, where she bears Civakan, laments the royal birth he should have had and the deeds she blames for it, takes refuge in the Jina's dharma, and is met by a deity in her maid's form who foretells that someone will come for the child and bids her hide.

294.reading: The black-hearted usurper sees the dead king lying like a lion on a soft couch ringed by peacocks, joins his hands and sheds tears; then, as ghee pots by the hundred are poured on the blazing pyre, the women wail, asking their lord whether he has hidden himself from them.
294.nuance: The poet's label கரிமாலை நெஞ்சினான் turns the usurper's worship and tears into a show; who pours the ghee and who wails (the usurper's men or the king's women) is not plain in the run of participles.
294.event: Kattiyankaran weeps over the dead king and the body is burned while the women wail.

295.reading: The bangled women beat their bangles, tear the necklaces from their breasts, strip garlands, earrings and ear-drops and throw them down, press their bellies, cry 'my lord' and say the cruelty the king has done is cruel.
295.nuance: வேந்தன் செய்த கொடுமை may blame the new ruler's deed or reproach the dead king for leaving them; the verse does not say which king.
295.event: The king's women cast off their ornaments in mourning.

296.reading: Like young she-elephants on a red hillside grieving when a hooded snake has felled their tusker, the women go weeping, saying they will come to that world and reach his feet, and that this creeper which flowered when their lord plucked it will never flower again for others to pluck.
296.nuance: போயினார் leaves open whether the women go to their deaths on the pyre or only depart in grief; the vow to reach his feet in the other world points to the first.
296.event: The king's women resolve to follow him to the other world and leave weeping.

claims.claim: a wife who flowered for her husband will not flower for another after his death

297.reading: Like a red-eyed jackal that has killed a lion and taken its den, the usurper threw the spear-bearing king into the fire, went off and had the drum beaten in his own name from an elephant's back; at that rain of spears, 'our husbands too' grieved, and the dark-minded man took Fortune.
297.nuance: எம் கணவரும் puts the verse in the mouth of the city's women, or of the poet speaking with the people; the jackal-and-lion simile makes the seizure unnatural, not only cruel.
297.event: Kattiyankaran has himself proclaimed king by drum, and the people grieve.

298.reading: The poet turns to tell what befell the parrot-voiced queen who, her garland slipping from her neck and her mind unsteady as a flame in the wind, had gone by the path her elephant-like husband bade her take.

299.reading: As the victory drum of the man whose fame was coveted roared, the sword-eyed queen, by the strength now worn thin in her, riding the fine peacock, faints like a doe struck by a spear and sinks senseless.
299.event: Hearing the usurper's victory drum, Vijayai faints on the flying peacock.

300.reading: Leaving the high-built city, the peacock with its lovely plumes slowly comes down where old trees crowd, corpses lie heaped to daunt even the stout-hearted, and vultures sleep in the shade across the whole forest.
300.event: The mechanical peacock carries Vijayai out of the city and sinks into the burning ground.

301.reading: In that burning ground, thick with corpse-smoke like gathering cloud and feared even by ghosts, the crested peacock falls as a garland falls on cotton and settles with folded feet.
301.event: The peacock lands in the cremation ground.

302.reading: Her tears wetting her breasts, the queen of peacock grace feels no fear in that sea-wide forest; she grieves and sighs for her lord, cannot even set right her slipping garment, and is like a magandril parted from its mate.
302.nuance: ஏல் பெற்று is obscure; it may say she had come to her time. Grief for the king, not fear of the place, fills her: the poet makes loss outweigh terror.

303.reading: As if to show those who hear only in words that sin exists, and bid them see it now and be sure of all the sin that clings to lives, she who once went into sky-touching palaces like a heavenly maiden is left alone in a forest of white skulls.
303.nuance: The poet frames the queen as an exhibit (காட்டுவாள் போல), so her fall is offered as visible proof of an unseen law; the verse does not say whose sin, and does not blame her.
303.event: Vijayai is left alone in the burning ground.

claims.claim: the sin that clings to lives, known to most only by hearsay, can be seen in a reversal of fortune

304.reading: The moment the golden child is born, like the sun from the surging sea, gem lamps blaze all round driving out the dark, the deities of the place bow with gracious hearts, and the bewildered mother's distress vanishes.
304.nuance: The burning ground's own deities (அணங்கு) turn from dread to worship at the birth, so the place of death becomes a birth-hall for a hero.
304.event: Civakan is born in the burning ground, and the deities there light lamps and bow.

305.reading: Looking with longing at the son her warrior lord had given her, the queen's young breasts swell and milk flows like moonlight; unable to bear it she takes him up, sets a tilaka on him and lays the jewel of a child down with care.
305.nuance: திலகம் சேர்த்தி may be the forehead mark or a token of the king set beside the child; the verse plays on திலகம் and திலகன்.
305.event: Vijayai nurses and marks her newborn son.

306.reading: The queen voices the orders the birth should have brought: remit dues for twelve years, set up fair halls and shrines, clear the prisons where hostile kings lie like caged lions, open the gold hoards and give in every town to all who will take, saying the king's son is born.
306.nuance: The imperatives are those a court would send its heralds; spoken in a burning ground, the unsent proclamation measures what the child has lost.

307.reading: She goes on: proclaim that in the rich city all goods are thrown open, that for seven days anyone may take cloth, gold and jewels unchecked, and that the lord grants three and a half crores of gold to those who have fallen into want.
307.nuance: வீழ்ந்தீர்க்கு is read here as those fallen into want; it could mean those fallen in battle.

308.reading: Astrologers would gather in the wide palace to cast his horoscope, the glad news would go to kings, and elephants, blankets and coin be scattered for poets; 'I who did such deeds, see: is this how you, who should have been born amid longing, are born?'
308.nuance: Line 4 can also be read as 'I did deeds so that you would be born to be desired'; either way the mother ties the wretched birth to her own deeds.

claims.claim: a mother's own past deeds account for the wretched birth of her child

309.reading: With howling jackals for drums, pyres for lamps, ghosts swaying like shadows on the high stage of the unseemly burning ground, and owls hooting from every side as if in praise, she asks the child whether this is how he is born, whether this is the way of kings.
309.nuance: The burning ground is laid out as a mock birth-festival, its creatures taking the parts of drummers, lamp-bearers, dancers and praise-singers.

310.reading: Because this is the outskirts of a hostile king's city, a burning ground strewn with corpses, because she is alone without kin and the darkness is too thick to move in, she does not know how the child, lord of this earth, will grow, and she cries out that her sweet life stays on, though it sees all this.
310.nuance: என் இன் உயிரே may address her own life, which will not leave her, or the child; on the first reading she reproaches herself for surviving.

311.reading: If he who is born and the great dharma of the lord of the flowering asoka do not become her raft across the sea of sorrow, she asks whether anyone greater exists; calling the child 'Cintamani', she says she did as his fierce father bade, and asks whether she must now suffer in bewildered grief.
311.nuance: பூம் பிண்டிப் பெருமான், the lord beneath the asoka, is the Jina; the mother here gives her son the name the epic bears.

claims.claim: the dharma of the Jina is a raft across the sea of sorrow

312.reading: Alas, as Vijayai's lot turned like the palm to the back of the hand, with her lord gone and she come alone into the outer forest like a peacock riding a peacock, the trees seem to think on it and weep, shedding dewdrops as tears.

313.reading: The queen who had lost her kingdom and gained a golden son was like an evening whose distress is past, when the sun has drunk the world's darkness and set, and a young crescent moon cools the heart.

314.reading: As the queen sits grieving, not knowing what to do for her son, a deity takes the shape of the hunchbacked Sanbagamalai, who never left her side, and comes near.
314.event: A deity comes to Vijayai in the form of her maid Sanbagamalai.

315.reading: When the deity of that place draws near, the queen sighs and the whirling care in her heart lifts; and the deity, as the maid, says that her lady's being alone and meeting all this sorrow is the maid's own sin.
315.nuance: The speaker of lines 3 and 4 may instead be Vijayai, blaming her own sin for the maid's hardship; the vocative செம் மலர்த் திருவின் பாவாய் suits a servant addressing the queen. Set against 308, the self-blame here is a servant's, for a lapse of service.
315.event: The disguised deity comforts Vijayai and takes the blame for her solitude.

316.reading: The deity tells the queen that this prince, like the holy one born among flowers, at whose word the whole world will move, is to crush the king who stands against him; one will come right now and take him away, and it is their part to hide.
316.nuance: Whether the crushing of the hostile king belongs to the child or to the man who will come is not fixed by the word order; the story gives it to the child. பூவினுள் பிறந்த தோன்றல் may be the lotus-born god or the Jina who walks on flowers.
316.event: The deity foretells that someone will come for the child and bids Vijayai hide.

links.note: Perunkoppendu argues against the elders that the widow's life of plain food and gravel beds is not for her and the pyre is a lotus pool; Saccandan's women make the same choice in a simile and a vow of the other world, without the argument.
links.teaches: Set beside the Sangam queen's reasoned refusal, the epic's wives choose death as a group and by figure alone, while the one queen who must live, Vijayai, is spared the choice by her unborn son.

gains.a: The epic verse gains the explicit alternative its women reject, the austere widow's life Purananuru 246 describes.
gains.b: The Purananuru poem gains a counter-case in the same scene: a queen (Vijayai) whom motherhood bars from the pyre.

links.note: Naladiyar 3 says kings who rode elephants under the umbrella fall when their deeds turn and enemies take their wives; here the usurper mounts the elephant to proclaim himself and takes Fortune.
links.teaches: The quatrain names only the fallen king, but the epic shows the other half of the turn: the enemy who rises on the same elephant, a figure the poem's logic marks for the next fall.

gains.a: The epic scene gains a general frame in which the usurper's elephant-back triumph is itself unstable.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a named winner and a cause the poem leaves out: the fallen king's own neglect of rule.

links.note: Kural 37 bids the reader look at palanquin-bearer and rider instead of being told what virtue is; 303 offers the queen alone among skulls as sight for those who know sin only by report.
links.teaches: Both turn visible fortune into evidence for unseen merit, but the epic applies it to one life reversed from palace to burning ground, and the proof falls on a sufferer the poet does not blame.

gains.a: The epic's 'as if to show' gains the general argument from sight that Kural 37 states.
gains.b: The couplet gains a case where rider and bearer are the same person in one life, which exposes the cost of reading misfortune as proof.

links.note: Manimekalai 6 lists young mothers just delivered and helpless infants among those Death heaps for the burning ground to eat; in the Cintamani a mother gives birth in the burning ground and its deities bow.
links.teaches: The Buddhist epic makes the burning ground the end that spares no new mother or infant, while the Jain epic makes the same ground the birthplace of a king, so the place teaches impermanence in one and providence in the other.

links.note: Purananuru 359 gives the burning ground of owls, corpse-eating jackals and ghoul-women dancing by pyre lamps that has received even conquerors; 309 has jackals as drums, pyres as lamps, ghosts dancing and owls praising at a prince's birth.
links.teaches: The same creatures and lights that in the Sangam poem greet the end of kings serve in the epic as the band and lamps of a future king's birth, turning a warning about death into a grim birth-festival.

gains.a: Vijayai's bitter question gains its weight from the old image of this ground as where kingdoms end.
gains.b: The Sangam image gains a reversal it never shows: the ground receiving a beginning rather than an end.

links.note: Kural 10: only those who reach the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births. Vijayai asks that the Jina's dharma and her newborn son be her raft across a sea of sorrow.
links.teaches: The epic keeps the Kural's sea and crossing but moves the sea from rebirth to present grief and doubles the raft, placing a mother's hope in a child beside the lord's dharma.

gains.a: Vijayai's plea gains the doctrinal sea and swimmer the couplet fixes.
gains.b: The couplet gains a human raft alongside the divine one, which it does not allow for.

links.note: In 269 Saccandan consoles Vijayai that birth and death come from one's own deeds and that grief shows want of understanding; at the birth she blames her own deeds for the child's wretched birth and grieves.
links.teaches: The doctrine the king offered to end her grief becomes, once he is gone, the ground of her self-accusation, so the same teaching consoles the dying and burdens the survivor.

links.note: Vijayai's dream in 223 showed the asoka tree falling and a crowned shoot rising from its foot; 313 shows her as an evening where the sun has set and a young moon has risen.
links.teaches: The fall Saccandan would not interpret in 225 is now fulfilled, and the poet restates the dream's double meaning, loss and rising heir, in a new figure of sun and crescent moon.

links.note: The patikam in 10 says a deity stood at the mother's shoulder as companion and ended her distress; 314 shows how: the deity comes in the shape of the hunchbacked maid who never left her.
links.teaches: The summary's 'divine companion' turns out to work through disguise, choosing the most familiar servant's form, so the help comes as continuity of the queen's household rather than as a marvel.

links.note: The deity foretells that one will come right now to take the child and bids the queen hide; in 322 Kantukkatan reaches the child lying in the burning ground.
links.teaches: The prophecy and the command to hide make the mother's absence in 322 an arranged handing-over, not a desertion, which the finding scene alone would not show.

cast.role: king of Emangatham, Civakan's father, now dead and burned
Saccandan's minister who has usurped the throne
the hero, born in the burning ground
the king's women, who mourn him
the women of the city, who speak of 'our husbands' grieving
the deities of the burning ground, who bow at the birth
the deity who stands by Vijayai at the burning ground, in the form of her maid Sanbagamalai

source_issues: Verses 294 to 297 and 299 to 313 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four by the build (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.
Verse 294 runs participles across lines 2 to 4 so that the subject of the ghee-pouring and wailing is unclear.
Verse 302 line 1 ஏல் பெற்று is obscure as printed.
Verse 315: the speaker of lines 3 and 4 (deity in maid's form or Vijayai) is not marked in the text.
